title: Who Knows What—and What Does It Support?Perspective-Bounded Evidence Calibration for Multimodal Theory of Mind

paper.title: Who Knows What—and What Does It Support? Perspective-Bounded Evidence Calibration for Multimodal Theory of Mind
paper.abstract:
Abstract Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer others’ beliefs, goals, and intentions, is a cornerstone of social intelligence.
Multimodal ToM requires inferring an agent’s mental state from evidence that is available to that agent, rather than from the complete episode observed by the solver.
Existing LLM-based and Bayesian model-based
approaches reconstruct global event traces, yet they do not explicitly distinguish objective events from agent-admissible evidence during hypothesis evaluation. Consequently, agent-inaccessible events or semantically misaligned actions and utterances may influence the inferred belief, goal, or social intention, leading to perspective leakage and source or route confusion.
We formulate this limitation as an evidence-admissibility problem: evidence should contribute to a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant agent, preserves its information source, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable.
To operationalize this principle, we propose PIP-ToM, an evidence-admissibility interface that constructs
agent-specific evidence stores, aligns them with structured mental-state claims, and calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process.
PIP-ToM with GPT-4o outperforms existing ToM methods across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, achieving average accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%, respectively.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Multimodal Theory of Mind (ToM) asks a globally informed solver to infer the beliefs, goals, intentions, and communicative motives of an agent who has observed only part of an unfolding episode. This ability is a central component of social intelligence ( Wellman 2018 ; Beaudoin et al. 2020 ; Zhang et al. 2026a ; Zhang et al. 2026b ; Zhang et al. 2025a ; Chen et al. 2025 ; Zhong et al. 2026 ) . In interactive environments, relevant evidence is distributed across visual observations, object interactions, actions, communication, and memory, while different agents have access to different subsets of the same event history. The central challenge is therefore not merely to reconstruct what happened in the objective world, but to determine which evidence was available to the queried agent and which mental-state hypotheses that evidence can legitimately support. Figure 1: An example showing that an agent’s utterance must be interpreted together with the agent’s belief to support correct mental-state inference. Figure 1 provides a motivating example of why interpreting an agent’s utterance without considering the agent’s belief is insufficient for ToM inference. A model may interpret Jessica’s act of providing a location as an attempt to help without considering what she knows. Jessica knows that the magazine is on the table, yet tells Kevin that it is in the bedroom cabinet; Kevin subsequently searches the cabinet and finds nothing. Inferring Jessica’s social goal therefore requires moving beyond what happened to determine who knows what and what that belief supports . Specifically, the solver must recover Jessica’s belief at the time of speaking, preserve her utterance as a source-tagged communicative act, and infer how the utterance was intended to affect Kevin’s search. Existing approaches address important components of this problem through explicit state tracking, perspective reconstruction, and model-based hypothesis scoring ( Wilf et al. 2024 ; Jung et al. 2024 ; Huang et al. 2024 ; Xu et al. 2025 ; Zhu et al. 2026 ; Zhang et al. 2025b ) . However, the interface between agent-relative evidence reconstruction and candidate hypothesis scoring remains under-specified. Models must determine whether evidence is accessible to the relevant perspective holder and whether that evidence can legitimately support the queried mental-state variable. Insufficient control over evidence accessibility may allow globally reconstructed but agent-inaccessible events to influence hypothesis evaluation, resulting in perspective leakage . Insufficient control over evidential relevance may cause accessible evidence to support the wrong belief, goal, communicative effect, or recursive mental state, leading to source or route confusion . We collectively refer to these failures as evidence inadmissibility . The central issue is therefore not only whether events are reconstructed correctly, but also whether each piece of evidence is assigned to the appropriate epistemic owner and evidential role. This motivates an explicit constraint on when evidence may legitimately influence a mental-state hypothesis. Figure 1 illustrates a concrete manifestation of this missing constraint: reconstructing the global episode does not itself determine which evidence may legitimately influence Jessica’s social-goal hypothesis. We formulate this constraint as an Evidence Admissibility Principle . Evidence may directly support or contradict a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant perspective holder, is represented with its source preserved, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. Accordingly, inaccessible information should be treated as missing evidence, while accessible but claim-irrelevant information should not directly alter the corresponding hypothesis score. Based on this principle, we introduce PIP-ToM , an evidence-admissibility interface for Bayesian and model-based multimodal ToM inference. Given a fused episode trace, PIP-ToM constructs agent-specific perspective stores, parses candidates into structured mental-state claims, and routes accessible evidence according to claim type. It then maps claim–evidence compatibility to a bounded calibration factor that adjusts the corresponding hypothesis likelihood, making evidence ownership and evidential relevance explicit during mental-state inference. Our contributions are threefold: • We identify an under-specified interface between agent-relative evidence reconstruction and mental-state hypothesis evaluation, and formulate an Evidence Admissibility Principle that constrains evidence by accessibility, source preservation, and claim-specific relevance. • We introduce PIP-ToM, a perspective-bounded evidence-calibration framework that operationalizes this principle by jointly constraining evidence accessibility and its relevance to the queried mental-state hypothesis. • Experiments across three benchmarks and multiple backbones demonstrate consistent improvements. Ablation analyses show that evidence accessibility and claim-specific relevance address complementary failure modes, while direct-posterior diagnostics reveal the limits of structured evidence matching for latent and recursive mental-state reasoning.

sections.heading: Explicit State Tracking
sections.text: Explicit state reconstruction provides a factual foundation for subsequent ToM reasoning. Discrete World Models ( Huang et al. 2024 ) represent narratives as event-driven transitions over compact world states. EnigmaToM ( Xu et al. 2025 ) augments these representations with entity-state knowledge and spatial scene graphs. This design connects global scene reconstruction with perspective masking and higher-order belief tracking. PDDL-Mind ( Zhu et al. 2026 ) instead maps narratives to a predefined PDDL domain, verifying action preconditions and effects while recording agents’ event access through predicates such as seen and heard . These methods transform unstructured narratives into structured global state trajectories, thereby providing a basis for moving from global event reconstruction to agent-specific knowledge inference.

sections.heading: Perspective Reconstruction
sections.text: After reconstructing the global event sequence, perspective reconstruction extracts the information available to a specific agent. SimToM ( Wilf et al. 2024 ) and PercepToM ( Jung et al. 2024 ) isolate information observable to a target agent, with PercepToM further separating perception extraction from belief inference. Other work moves beyond static information filtering by maintaining structured mental-state representations over time. TimeToM ( Hou et al. 2024 ) organizes temporally evolving belief states, while SymbolicToM ( Sclar et al. 2023 ) tracks multiple characters and their higher-order beliefs in graph-based representations, and ThoughtTracing ( Kim et al. 2025 ) propagates and reweights natural-language hypotheses about an agent’s evolving mental state. This line of work converts global event trajectories into agent-relative representations, reducing objective-state leakage into belief inference while supporting candidate comparison.

sections.heading: Bayesian and Model-Based Mental-State Inference
sections.text: Given an agent-relative representation, Bayesian and model-based approaches infer latent mental states that explain observed behavior. Classical Bayesian ToM ( Baker et al. 2009 ; Baker et al. 2017 ; Jara-Ettinger 2019 ) frames this process as inverse planning over beliefs, desires, percepts, goals, and actions. Recent systems ( Jin et al. 2024 ; Shi et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2025a ) extend this framework to multimodal settings, social interaction, and longer reasoning chains, while AutoToM ( Zhang et al. 2025b ) discovers task-specific mental variables and dependencies and MindZero ( Zhang et al. 2026c ) learns online mental-state reasoning without explicit annotation. Prior work thus reconstructs global states, derives agent-specific perspectives, and infers candidate mental states. However, it leaves a key interface under-specified: which agent-accessible evidence may legitimately affect the likelihood of a given mental-state hypothesis? This gap motivates treating evidence admissibility as an explicit modeling problem between perspective reconstruction and model-based inference. Figure 2: Overview of PIP-ToM. It transforms a fused episode trace and candidate answers into perspective-bounded evidence, route-specific factors, and a final answer posterior.

sections.heading: Overview of PIP-ToM
sections.text: Multimodal ToM requires reasoning over evolving multimodal evidence to infer agents’ mental states under partial observability. Among existing approaches, Bayesian inverse planning ( Baker et al. 2009 ; Baker et al. 2017 ; Jara-Ettinger 2019 ) provides a principled model-based framework that reasons backward from observed behavior to the beliefs, goals, and intentions that could have generated it. However, when inference is performed over a globally reconstructed episode, it remains unclear which observations, actions, or utterances should be admissible for evaluating a particular agent’s mental state. Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of PIP-ToM. The framework first constructs an Agent-Specific Perspective Storage, then parses candidate answers through a Structured Mental-State Schema, and finally applies route-specific evidence calibration to the local scores used for hypothesis evaluation. By operating at the evidence-to-score interface, PIP-ToM separates evidence ownership from evidential role without requiring a solver-specific redesign of the latent-state model.

sections.text: The Agent-Specific Perspective Storage provides the primary epistemic interface for organizing reconstructed events into agent-centered evidence views. In practice, the admission cues are instantiated from reconstructed timeline fields and source tags, and the resulting store renders an agent-scoped evidence view for downstream scoring. This organization reduces direct reliance on objective world-state facts when forming agent-centered scores and prevents intermediate belief estimates from being treated as observations. Perspective stores therefore organize evidence rather than assert oracle mental states.

sections.heading: Benchmarks
sections.text: We evaluate PIP-ToM on three ToM benchmarks: MuMA-ToM ( Shi et al. 2025 ) , MMToM-QA ( Jin et al. 2024 ) , and Hi-ToM ( Wu et al. 2023 ) . Detailed descriptions of the task settings, dataset sizes, and model configurations are provided in Supplementary Sec. B.

sections.heading: Baselines
sections.text: We compare PIP-ToM against state-of-the-art baselines: • General-purpose MLLMs: GPT-4o ( OpenAI 2024 ) , GPT-5.4 ( OpenAI 2026 ) , Qwen3-VL-8B ( Bai et al. 2025 ) , and InternVL3.5-8B ( Wang et al. 2025 ) . • ToM-specific Reasoning Prompting Methods: SimToM ( Wilf et al. 2024 ) and ThoughtTracing ( Kim et al. 2025 ) . • State Tracking Methods: DWM ( Huang et al. 2024 ) and PDDL-Mind ( Zhu et al. 2026 ) . • Model-based Inference: BIP-ALM ( Jin et al. 2024 ) , LIMP ( Shi et al. 2025 ) , and AutoToM ( Zhang et al. 2025b ) . To ensure a fair comparison, PIP-ToM uses the same fused video-text event traces as AutoToM ( Zhang et al. 2025b ) . sections.heading: Performance across Tasks and Reasoning Complexity
sections.text: Table 1 presents the main results. With GPT-4o, PIP-ToM outperforms AutoToM on MuMA-ToM (92.56% vs. 81.44%), with the largest gain on belief-of-goal reasoning (96.67% vs. 79.00%). It also raises average accuracy from 83.00% to 95.00% on MMToM-QA and from 72.50% to 95.00% on Hi-ToM. The improvements also persist across both open-source backbones, indicating that the gains arise from the proposed reasoning scaffold rather than from a particular proprietary model. Figure Baselines further breaks down performance across task types and reasoning orders.

sections.heading: Accuracy-Compute Trade-off
sections.text: Figure 4 compares accuracy and average inference-token consumption across the three benchmarks. Under matched backbones, PIP-ToM generally achieves higher accuracy at comparable or lower token costs. These differences may partly reflect variations in task structure and reasoning depth: MMToM-QA primarily involves single-agent reasoning, whereas MuMA-ToM and Hi-ToM require richer social and recursive mental-state reasoning. Overall, PIP-ToM maintains a favorable balance between accuracy and inference cost across diverse reasoning settings. sections.heading: Analysis by Research Questions
sections.text: We further analyze the effectiveness of PIP-ToM through three research questions: whether agent-specific evidence boundaries reduce interference from global information ( RQ1 ), whether claim-aware evidence routing and calibration align admissible evidence with the mental-state variables it can support ( RQ2 ), and whether perspective-conditioned evidence matching alone is sufficient across different mental-state reasoning tasks ( RQ3 ). sections.heading: RQ1: Perspective-Bounded Evidence
sections.text: To test whether agent-specific boundaries limit interference from inaccessible global events, we compare the Full model with the w/o Perspective Storage variant in Table 2 . Removing the perspective boundary lowers average accuracy, particularly on MMToM-QA. Figure 5 further shows that this effect is selective rather than uniform. The largest gains from Perspective Storage occur on tasks in which the agent’s information state may diverge from the objective episode state, including false-belief goal inference, belief updating, future-action prediction, cross-agent goal attribution, and higher-order belief reasoning. By contrast, performance changes little on true-belief and order-0 tasks, where agent-relative and global information largely align. Moreover, using predefined criteria, we manually audited 121 cases solved only by the GPT-4o Full model and found that the ablated predictions relied on inaccessible or global evidence in 62.8% of them; audit details are provided in Supplementary Sec. C. Takeaway 1: Perspective-bounded evidence reduces global-information interference in perspective-sensitive ToM reasoning.

sections.heading: RQ2: Claim-Aware Evidence Calibration
sections.text: To examine the role of claim-aware evidence calibration, we compare the Full model with the w/o Claim-Aware Calibration variant. As shown in Table 2 , this ablation causes the largest overall decline. Accuracy drops from 84.33% to 67.67% on MuMA-ToM Social Goal and from 90.33% to 70.50% on MMToM-QA Goal, with smaller reductions on explicit belief questions. Because claim-aware routing introduces bounded calibration factors, we additionally test whether these gains depend on the exact scale of the calibration factors. We further rescale all active factors using α ∈ { 0.75 , 1.0 , 1.25 } \alpha\in\{0.75,1.0,1.25\} with GPT-5.4. Across the weak and strong settings, the mean absolute deviations from the reference configuration are only 1.06 percentage points on MuMA-ToM and 1.09 percentage points on MMToM-QA. Takeaway 2: Evidence accessibility alone is insufficient; claim-aware routing is critical for goal and social reasoning.

sections.heading: Qualitative Case Studies
sections.text: Figure 6: Qualitative effects of the two components. Case 1 shows that perspective storage prevents inaccessible global facts from influencing inference. Case 2 shows that claim-aware routing prevents accessible evidence from being misused. Figure 6 explains why the two components provide complementary gains. The central issue is not whether the episode contains sufficient context, but whether each piece of evidence is used under the correct epistemic and semantic constraints. Perspective boundaries determine what evidence is accessible to the target agent, while claim-aware routing determines which mental-state variable that evidence can legitimately support. Together, these constraints ensure that posterior updates are calibrated using agent-accessible evidence that is relevant to the queried mental state. The gains therefore arise from a principled interface between global episode reconstruction and model-based latent-state inference, rather than from additional context.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we introduce PIP-ToM, a perspective-bounded evidence calibration framework for multimodal ToM. Given a globally reconstructed episode, PIP-ToM determines which evidence was accessible to the queried agent, identifies how that evidence may legitimately support a particular mental-state hypothesis, and calibrates the corresponding likelihoods while preserving the underlying model-based inference process. Experiments on MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM demonstrate consistent improvements across both closed- and open-source backbones. Our analyses further show that evidence accessibility and claim-specific relevance address complementary sources of error, while structured evidence matching alone remains insufficient for goal and recursive mental-state inference. These findings suggest that reliable ToM reasoning requires not only reconstructing what happened, but also tracking which agents had access to that information and how it should influence the inferred mental state.

Perspective-Bounded Evidence Calibration for Multimodal Theory of Mind Ziqi Liao Jiaqi Shen Yiming Na Kedi Lyu Shao-Yuan Lo Hongxia Xie Abstract Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer others’ beliefs, goals, and intentions, is a cornerstone of social intelligence. Multimodal ToM requires inferring an agent’s mental state from evidence that is available to that agent, rather than from the complete episode observed by the solver. Existing LLM-based and Bayesian model-based approaches reconstruct global event traces, yet they do not explicitly distinguish objective events from agent-admissible evidence during hypothesis evaluation. Consequently, agent-inaccessible events or semantically misaligned actions and utterances may influence the inferred belief, goal, or social intention, leading to perspective leakage and source or route confusion. We formulate this limitation as an evidence-admissibility problem: evidence should contribute to a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant agent, preserves its information source, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. To operationalize this principle, we propose PIP-ToM, an evidence-admissibility interface that constructs agent-specific evidence stores, aligns them with structured mental-state claims, and calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process. PIP-ToM with GPT-4o outperforms existing ToM methods across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, achieving average accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%, respectively. 1 Jilin University 2 National Taiwan University Introduction Multimodal Theory of Mind (ToM) asks a globally informed solver to infer the beliefs, goals, intentions, and communicative motives of an agent who has observed only part of an unfolding episode. This ability is a central component of social intelligence ( Wellman 2018 ; Beaudoin et al. 2020 ; Zhang et al. 2026a ; Zhang et al. 2026b ; Zhang et al. 2025a ; Chen et al. 2025 ; Zhong et al. 2026 ) . In interactive environments, relevant evidence is distributed across visual observations, object interactions, actions, communication, and memory, while different agents have access to different subsets of the same event history. The central challenge is therefore not merely to reconstruct what happened in the objective world, but to determine which evidence was available to the queried agent and which mental-state hypotheses that evidence can legitimately support. Figure 1: An example showing that an agent’s utterance must be interpreted together with the agent’s belief to support correct mental-state inference. Figure 1 provides a motivating example of why interpreting an agent’s utterance without considering the agent’s belief is insufficient for ToM inference. A model may interpret Jessica’s act of providing a location as an attempt to help without considering what she knows. Jessica knows that the magazine is on the table, yet tells Kevin that it is in the bedroom cabinet; Kevin subsequently searches the cabinet and finds nothing. Inferring Jessica’s social goal therefore requires moving beyond what happened to determine who knows what and what that belief supports . Specifically, the solver must recover Jessica’s belief at the time of speaking, preserve her utterance as a source-tagged communicative act, and infer how the utterance was intended to affect Kevin’s search. Existing approaches address important components of this problem through explicit state tracking, perspective reconstruction, and model-based hypothesis scoring ( Wilf et al. 2024 ; Jung et al. 2024 ; Huang et al. 2024 ; Xu et al. 2025 ; Zhu et al. 2026 ; Zhang et al. 2025b ) . However, the interface between agent-relative evidence reconstruction and candidate hypothesis scoring remains under-specified. Models must determine whether evidence is accessible to the relevant perspective holder and whether that evidence can legitimately support the queried mental-state variable. Insufficient control over evidence accessibility may allow globally reconstructed but agent-inaccessible events to influence hypothesis evaluation, resulting in perspective leakage . Insufficient control over evidential relevance may cause accessible evidence to support the wrong belief, goal, communicative effect, or recursive mental state, leading to source or route confusion . We collectively refer to these failures as evidence inadmissibility . The central issue is therefore not only whether events are reconstructed correctly, but also whether each piece of evidence is assigned to the appropriate epistemic owner and evidential role. This motivates an explicit constraint on when evidence may legitimately influence a mental-state hypothesis. Figure 1 illustrates a concrete manifestation of this missing constraint: reconstructing the global episode does not itself determine which evidence may legitimately influence Jessica’s social-goal hypothesis. We formulate this constraint as an Evidence Admissibility Principle . Evidence may directly support or contradict a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant perspective holder, is represented with its source preserved, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. Accordingly, inaccessible information should be treated as missing evidence, while accessible but claim-irrelevant information should not directly alter the corresponding hypothesis score. Based on this principle, we introduce PIP-ToM , an evidence-admissibility interface for Bayesian and model-based multimodal ToM inference. Given a fused episode trace, PIP-ToM constructs agent-specific perspective stores, parses candidates into structured mental-state claims, and routes accessible evidence according to claim type. It then maps claim–evidence compatibility to a bounded calibration factor that adjusts the corresponding hypothesis likelihood, making evidence ownership and evidential relevance explicit during mental-state inference. Our contributions are threefold: • We identify an under-specified interface between agent-relative evidence reconstruction and mental-state hypothesis evaluation, and formulate an Evidence Admissibility Principle that constrains evidence by accessibility, source preservation, and claim-specific relevance. • We introduce PIP-ToM, a perspective-bounded evidence-calibration framework that operationalizes this principle by jointly constraining evidence accessibility and its relevance to the queried mental-state hypothesis. • Experiments across three benchmarks and multiple backbones demonstrate consistent improvements. Ablation analyses show that evidence accessibility and claim-specific relevance address complementary failure modes, while direct-posterior diagnostics reveal the limits of structured evidence matching for latent and recursive mental-state reasoning. Related Work Explicit State Tracking Explicit state reconstruction provides a factual foundation for subsequent ToM reasoning. Discrete World Models ( Huang et al. 2024 ) represent narratives as event-driven transitions over compact world states. EnigmaToM ( Xu et al. 2025 ) augments these representations with entity-state knowledge and spatial scene graphs. This design connects global scene reconstruction with perspective masking and higher-order belief tracking. PDDL-Mind ( Zhu et al. 2026 ) instead maps narratives to a predefined PDDL domain, verifying action preconditions and effects while recording agents’ event access through predicates such as seen and heard . These methods transform unstructured narratives into structured global state trajectories, thereby providing a basis for moving from global event reconstruction to agent-specific knowledge inference. Perspective Reconstruction After reconstructing the global event sequence, perspective reconstruction extracts the information available to a specific agent. SimToM ( Wilf et al. 2024 ) and PercepToM ( Jung et al. 2024 ) isolate information observable to a target agent, with PercepToM further separating perception extraction from belief inference. Other work moves beyond static information filtering by maintaining structured mental-state representations over time. TimeToM ( Hou et al. 2024 ) organizes temporally evolving belief states, while SymbolicToM ( Sclar et al. 2023 ) tracks multiple characters and their higher-order beliefs in graph-based representations, and ThoughtTracing ( Kim et al. 2025 ) propagates and reweights natural-language hypotheses about an agent’s evolving mental state. This line of work converts global event trajectories into agent-relative representations, reducing objective-state leakage into belief inference while supporting candidate comparison. Bayesian and Model-Based Mental-State Inference Given an agent-relative representation, Bayesian and model-based approaches infer latent mental states that explain observed behavior. Classical Bayesian ToM ( Baker et al. 2009 ; Baker et al. 2017 ; Jara-Ettinger 2019 ) frames this process as inverse planning over beliefs, desires, percepts, goals, and actions. Recent systems ( Jin et al. 2024 ; Shi et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2025a ) extend this framework to multimodal settings, social interaction, and longer reasoning chains, while AutoToM ( Zhang et al. 2025b ) discovers task-specific mental variables and dependencies and MindZero ( Zhang et al. 2026c ) learns online mental-state reasoning without explicit annotation. Prior work thus reconstructs global states, derives agent-specific perspectives, and infers candidate mental states. However, it leaves a key interface under-specified: which agent-accessible evidence may legitimately affect the likelihood of a given mental-state hypothesis? This gap motivates treating evidence admissibility as an explicit modeling problem between perspective reconstruction and model-based inference. Figure 2: Overview of PIP-ToM. It transforms a fused episode trace and candidate answers into perspective-bounded evidence, route-specific factors, and a final answer posterior. Methodology Overview of PIP-ToM Multimodal ToM requires reasoning over evolving multimodal evidence to infer agents’ mental states under partial observability. Among existing approaches, Bayesian inverse planning ( Baker et al. 2009 ; Baker et al. 2017 ; Jara-Ettinger 2019 ) provides a principled model-based framework that reasons backward from observed behavior to the beliefs, goals, and intentions that could have generated it. However, when inference is performed over a globally reconstructed episode, it remains unclear which observations, actions, or utterances should be admissible for evaluating a particular agent’s mental state. Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of PIP-ToM. The framework first constructs an Agent-Specific Perspective Storage, then parses candidate answers through a Structured Mental-State Schema, and finally applies route-specific evidence calibration to the local scores used for hypothesis evaluation. By operating at the evidence-to-score interface, PIP-ToM separates evidence ownership from evidential role without requiring a solver-specific redesign of the latent-state model. Agent-Specific Perspective Storage The Agent-Specific Perspective Storage provides the primary epistemic interface for organizing reconstructed events into agent-centered evidence views. This is illustrated by the Mary–Michael example in Figure 2 . Mary’s request-related observations and her own utterance are retained in her storage, whereas Michael’s failed search in the fridge and later discovery in the dishwasher belong to Michael’s storage. In practice, the admission cues are instantiated from reconstructed timeline fields and source tags, and the resulting store renders an agent-scoped evidence view for downstream scoring. The interface distinguishes episode-level grounding context from the agent-scoped evidential view used for structured evidence calibration. The memory component carries forward admitted evidence and its source tags across timesteps. This organization reduces direct reliance on objective world-state facts when forming agent-centered scores and prevents intermediate belief estimates from being treated as observations. Perspective stores therefore organize evidence rather than assert oracle mental states. Structured Mental-State Schema Perspective reconstruction determines which evidence is accessible to an agent, but not how that evidence should be interpreted for a particular mental-state claim. The same event may play different evidential roles depending on the queried variable. For the running example in Figure 2 , Mary’s utterance is a communicative act rather than an objective update to the world state. Its role is evaluated with evidence supporting the speaker’s belief and evidence about its expected effect on the listener. PIP-ToM therefore represents each candidate as a typed mental-state claim rather than evaluating its surface text directly. Case 2 shows that claim-aware routing prevents accessible evidence from being misused. Figure 6 explains why the two components provide complementary gains. The central issue is not whether the episode contains sufficient context, but whether each piece of evidence is used under the correct epistemic and semantic constraints. Perspective boundaries determine what evidence is accessible to the target agent, while claim-aware routing determines which mental-state variable that evidence can legitimately support. Together, these constraints ensure that posterior updates are calibrated using agent-accessible evidence that is relevant to the queried mental state. The gains therefore arise from a principled interface between global episode reconstruction and model-based latent-state inference, rather than from additional context. Conclusion In this paper, we introduce PIP-ToM, a perspective-bounded evidence calibration framework for multimodal ToM. Given a globally reconstructed episode, PIP-ToM determines which evidence was accessible to the queried agent, identifies how that evidence may legitimately support a particular mental-state hypothesis, and calibrates the corresponding likelihoods while preserving the underlying model-based inference process. Experiments on MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM demonstrate consistent improvements across both closed- and open-source backbones. Our analyses further show that evidence accessibility and claim-specific relevance address complementary sources of error, while structured evidence matching alone remains insufficient for goal and recursive mental-state inference. These findings suggest that reliable ToM reasoning requires not only reconstructing what happened, but also tracking which agents had access to that information and how it should influence the inferred mental state.
